phases.title: Getting Started: Mindset & Environment
phases.subtitle: Before your first command, know why you're doing this and what you're doing it with

days.title: Why bug bounty? The real path into this career
days.task: Read Yashar Shahinzadeh's full post 'How to Become a Hacker'. Start a Notion/Obsidian vault and write down your real motivation for this path — you'll revisit and update this document throughout the whole roadmap.

resources.t: Yashar Shahinzadeh's blog — How to Become a Hacker
Voorivex Team — Bug Bounty Roadmap from Scratch

days.title: Watch Yashar Shahinzadeh's roadmap video
days.task: Watch the full roadmap video and take notes. Turn every recommendation into a checklist item in your personal doc.

days.title: Set up a Linux VM and hacking environment
days.task: Install VirtualBox/VMware and spin up Kali Linux or Parrot OS in a VM. Take an initial snapshot so you can always roll back a broken environment.

days.title: Create profiles on bug bounty platforms
days.task: Sign up on HackerOne and Bugcrowd, browse Hacktivity on both to see the format of public reports and what gets accepted. Read at least 5 real disclosed reports end to end.

days.title: Documentation tooling and your personal methodology
days.task: Build an Obsidian (or Notion) vault with folders: Methodology, CVE/Writeups, Targets, Reports. Start logging everything you learn from today — this habit is the single most valuable asset of a professional hunter.

phases.title: Linux & the Command Line
phases.subtitle: Without terminal fluency you can't run any hacking tool correctly

days.title: Linux basics: filesystem and core commands + OverTheWire Bandit — levels 0-2
days.task: (1) Practice the 'Linux Basics' chapter: ls, cd, pwd, cat, cp, mv, rm, mkdir, man. Use man/--help instead of Google for every command. (2) SSH into the Bandit server (level0/level0, password: bandit0) and solve the first three levels. Learn to find hidden files, oddly named files, and command output.

days.title: Bandit — levels 3-6
days.task: Practice hidden files, recursive search with find, and filtering by type/size/permission. Combine find and grep.

days.title: Bandit — levels 7-10 + Permissions, ownership and environment variables
days.task: (1) Practice advanced grep, archive handling (tar/gzip/bzip2), and Base64/binary files. (2) Learn rwx, numeric/symbolic chmod, chown, and environment variables (PATH, env), then solve Bandit levels 11-14.

days.title: SSH keys, ports and processes
days.task: Generate an SSH key with ssh-keygen, connect with a private key, inspect running processes (ps, netstat/ss). Solve Bandit levels 15-18.

days.title: Cron jobs, setuid, and simple scripting
days.task: Understand cron, setuid binaries, and how a binary can run as a different user. Solve Bandit levels 19-23.

days.title: Netcat and basic network communication + Git from a security angle + unusual binaries
days.task: (1) Practice nc: opening a listening port, sending/receiving data, simulating a simple client-server. Solve Bandit levels 24-27. (2) Learn Git history, exposed .git/ repos, and recovering data from old commits — directly useful for finding exposed .git/ in bug bounty. Solve Bandit levels 28-31.

days.title: Bandit — levels 32-33 + wrap-up
days.task: Finish the remaining Bandit levels. Write a summary page in Obsidian: which Linux commands you learned and when you'd use them.

days.title: Bash scripting basics + Bash scripting — advanced automation
days.task: (1) Practice variables, loops (for/while), conditionals (if) and arguments. Write three small scripts: count files, ping a list of IPs, parse a text file. (2) Learn arrays, functions, and pipelines (|, xargs, tee). Write a script that reads a domain list and curls each one, printing HTTP status codes — the seed of your future recon scripts.

days.title: TryHackMe: Linux Fundamentals 2 and 3 (free)
days.task: Finish the next two Linux Fundamentals rooms: package management (apt), services (systemctl), and a text editor (nano/vim).

days.title: Review and self-test: Linux
days.task: Without notes, write down 10 important Linux commands from memory and explain their use. Revisit any topic you get stuck on.

phases.title: Networking & the HTTP Protocol
phases.subtitle: The web runs on HTTP; if you don't understand HTTP, you can't understand any web vulnerability

days.title: OSI and TCP/IP models + DNS from scratch
days.task: (1) Learn the OSI/TCP-IP layers, TCP vs UDP, and the concept of a port. Write the 7 OSI layers from memory in Obsidian. (2) Learn how DNS works, record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS), and dig/nslookup — test them on real domains.

days.title: HTTP from scratch — methods and status codes
days.task: Read MDN in full on GET/POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH/OPTIONS/HEAD, request/response structure, and status codes (2xx-5xx).

days.title: HTTP headers and cookies
days.task: Learn the important security headers (Cookie, Set-Cookie, Authorization, Content-Type, Host, Referer, Origin, CSP, HSTS). Open a real site with Burp or DevTools and identify every header of one request.

days.title: Install and set up Burp Suite Community + Hands-on Burp Suite: Proxy and Repeater
days.task: (1) Install Burp Suite Community (free), point your browser's proxy at it, install its CA certificate, and intercept your first HTTPS traffic. (2) Practice the Proxy and Repeater tabs against a test site (e.g. PortSwigger labs): intercept a request, send to Repeater, modify parameters, resend.

resources.t: PortSwigger — setting up Burp with Firefox

days.title: HTTPS/TLS in plain terms
days.task: Understand the TLS handshake, digital certificates, and why HTTPS blocks naive interception (conceptual level, not the math).

days.title: REST APIs and JSON
days.task: Learn APIs, REST, and JSON. Use Burp against a free public API (e.g. JSONPlaceholder) and rebuild GET/POST requests in Repeater.

days.title: Web servers: Apache and Nginx + Wireshark and network traffic analysis
days.task: (1) Learn the difference between Apache and Nginx, virtual hosts, reverse proxies, and basic config files — essential later for SSRF and request smuggling. (2) Install Wireshark and capture your own browser traffic. Find and inspect HTTP and DNS packets in it.

resources.t: DigitalOcean — free Apache vs Nginx comparison

days.title: Nmap: port and service scanning
days.task: Practice a basic nmap scan (-sV, -sC, -p-) against a legal target (e.g. scanme.nmap.org) and interpret the output.

days.title: TryHackMe: Web Fundamentals — How the Web Works
days.task: Finish the starter room of the Web Fundamentals path: browsers, servers, and the full lifecycle of a web request, from a security lens.

days.title: Mini project: map a full HTTP request
days.task: Draw a diagram (paper or Excalidraw) of the full path from a user's click to the response rendering: DNS → TCP handshake → TLS → HTTP request → server → response → browser render.

phases.title: Programming for Hackers
phases.subtitle: Python for scripting/automation, JavaScript for understanding and exploiting the client side

days.title: Python: variables, data types, conditionals + Python: loops and functions
days.task: (1) Read chapters 1-3 of the free book Automate the Boring Stuff and code the exercises. (2) Practice for/while loops and writing functions. Build a script that reads a word list and performs a simple operation on each (e.g. building input permutations).

resources.t: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python (free full book)
Automate the Boring Stuff — functions chapter

days.title: Python: lists, dictionaries, and file I/O
days.task: Learn lists, dicts, and reading/writing text files. Write a script that reads a wordlist from a file and removes duplicate lines.

resources.t: Automate the Boring Stuff — files chapter

days.title: Python: the requests library
days.task: Send a GET and a POST to a real API with requests, set custom headers/cookies, and parse the JSON response.

days.title: Python project: simple subdomain scanner + Python project: broken/open link checker
days.task: (1) Using requests and a small wordlist, write a script that checks a handful of common subdomains (www, api, dev, staging) on a test domain and prints each one's HTTP status. (2) Extend the previous script to run concurrently (threading or concurrent.futures) for speed — the foundation of your future recon tools.

days.title: JavaScript: language basics
days.task: Learn variables (let/const), functions, conditionals, and loops — all client-side web logic is written in this language.

days.title: JavaScript: the DOM and events
days.task: Learn DOM manipulation, event listeners, and innerHTML — this is exactly where XSS understanding begins.

days.title: JavaScript: Same-Origin Policy and Fetch/AJAX + SQL from scratch
days.task: (1) Learn Origin, the Same-Origin Policy, and how fetch/XMLHttpRequest work — the direct foundation of CORS and CSRF. (2) Learn SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, UNION, and comments in SQL with a free practice database — an absolute prerequisite for SQL injection.

days.title: Git and GitHub for hackers
days.task: Learn clone, commit, branch, and — more importantly — how to search public commit history for leaked secrets (API keys, passwords).

days.title: Phase capstone: personal recon tool v1
days.task: Combine everything from this phase into the first version of your personal recon tool: take a domain, check a few common subdomains, save output to CSV. You'll keep developing this tool throughout the roadmap.

resources.t: Build your own GitHub repo for it

days.title: Programming phase review
days.task: Without looking at old code, write a fresh Python script that takes a URL, checks its HTTP status, and prints the response headers. Revisit any topic you get stuck on.

phases.title: Web Security Fundamentals & Burp Suite
phases.subtitle: Before hunting, master the map of vulnerabilities and your core tool

days.title: OWASP Top 10 — full list + Modern web application architecture
days.task: (1) Read the full 2021 OWASP Top 10 and write a one-line explanation of each in your own words in Obsidian — this framework is the reference point for the rest of the roadmap. (2) Understand the difference between traditional server-rendered apps and SPAs (React/Vue/Angular), and the role of APIs in modern architecture — the attack surface differs for each.

days.title: Burp Suite: Intruder and basic fuzzing
days.task: Work through the Intruder tab against a practice target (DVWA or PortSwigger labs): Sniper, payload types, and analyzing results by response length.

days.title: Set up DVWA for local practice
days.task: Spin up DVWA (Damn Vulnerable Web Application) on your VM with XAMPP/Docker — a fully legal local environment for practicing techniques.

days.title: Burp Suite: Decoder, Comparer and Extensions
days.task: Learn Decoder for Base64/URL-encoding, practice Comparer for diffing two responses, and install a few free extensions from the BApp Store (e.g. Logger++).

days.title: General web pentest methodology + Start Yashar Shahinzadeh's free Maktabkhooneh course
days.task: (1) Learn the full cycle of a web security assessment (Recon → Mapping → Testing → Exploitation → Reporting) from Bugcrowd University's free materials. (2) Find Yashar Shahinzadeh's free 'Application Security from Scratch' course on Maktabkhooneh, enroll for free, and start watching.

resources.t: His X/Twitter for new course announcements

days.title: Start PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Essential Skills
days.task: Before diving into vulnerability classes, finish the Essential Skills section of PortSwigger Academy to learn how the labs and platform work.

days.title: Sign up for Hacker101 and start the videos
days.task: Sign up for Hacker101 (completely free, built by HackerOne) and watch the first introductory videos. You'll continue this alongside PortSwigger throughout the roadmap.

days.title: Review: full mind map of your progress so far
days.task: Draw a mind map of everything you've learned so far: Linux, networking, programming, tools. This is your foundation before entering the vulnerabilities phase.

phases.title: Core Web Vulnerabilities (PortSwigger Academy)
phases.subtitle: The heart of this roadmap: theory + free PortSwigger labs for every vulnerability class

days.title: SQL Injection — part 1 of 2
days.task: The king of server-side vulnerabilities; solve all 18 labs carefully, from UNION-based to time-delay blind. Today, solve roughly 9 labs from 'SQL Injection' on PortSwigger Academy on your own; if you're stuck after 30 minutes, only look at the hint, not the full solution. This is a real, long study session — not a quick drill, so budget the time. Write a short summary (what it was, how it was found, how it's fixed) in Obsidian for each vulnerability you solve.

days.title: Big review: rebuild every vulnerability on DVWA
days.task: On your local DVWA, implement at least one example of every vulnerability class you've learned (SQLi, XSS, CSRF, IDOR, SSRF...) from scratch, without looking at notes.

days.title: Big checkpoint: full Web Security Academy sweep
days.task: Go back to PortSwigger Academy's 'All Topics' page and finish any lab still unsolved. Goal: your Academy progress bar should be above 80%.

phases.title: Focused Practice: Voorivex & Hacker101 CTF
phases.subtitle: Time to put the theory to the test with focused Persian-community content and a real CTF

days.title: Finish Yashar Shahinzadeh's free course + Go through the Voorivex Team blog and socials
days.task: (1) Complete the 'Free Application Security from Scratch' course on Maktabkhooneh. Anything you've heard repeated but aren't sure about, look up again on PortSwigger. (2) Read every technical post on the Voorivex Team blog and follow Yashar Shahinzadeh on X for new writeups.

days.title: Note: Voorivex Academy courses are paid
days.task: Voorivex Academy's official courses (e.g. OWASP ZeroX) are paid live classes, not free — no need to register or pay. Just glance at the course page to see their curriculum structure for inspiration, and spend your time on the same founders' genuinely free YouTube/blog content instead.

resources.t: Voorivex Academy course page (for reference only)

days.title: Hacker101 CTF — sign up and first challenge + Hacker101 CTF — tier 2 challenges
days.task: (1) Sign up for Hacker101 CTF and solve the first (usually easiest) challenge without outside help. (2) Move to the more complex Hacker101 CTF challenges. Document every challenge in detail in Obsidian, solved or not — this is direct practice for writing professional reports.

days.title: Hacker101 CTF — advanced challenges
days.task: Work on the hardest remaining challenges. If you're genuinely stuck after real effort, search for public Hacker101 write-ups — but only read them after trying yourself.

days.title: Google XSS Game and Google Gruyere + OverTheWire Natas — levels 0-7 (web-specific wargame)
days.task: (1) Solve Google's two free practice environments; XSS Game focuses specifically on XSS and Gruyere is a full vulnerable app with varied challenges. (2) Unlike Bandit which is Linux-focused, Natas targets web vulnerabilities directly (View Source, PHP, cookies, headers). Solve levels 0-7 using your browser and View-Source.

days.title: OverTheWire Natas — levels 8-15
days.task: Solve the mid-tier Natas levels: PHP type-comparison bypasses, command injection, and simple logic bugs in PHP code.

days.title: HackTheBox — free account and Starting Point Tier 0 + HackTheBox — Starting Point Tier 1
days.task: (1) Create a free HackTheBox account (no VIP needed) and solve the Starting Point Tier 0 machines; each one ships with an official free step-by-step guide. (2) Move to Tier 1 machines; slightly more complex than Tier 0, and they build your service-enumeration skills and ability to chain multiple vulnerabilities.

days.title: Bugcrowd University — videos and labs
days.task: Watch any Bugcrowd University video modules you haven't seen yet, especially XSS, Access Control, and Burp Suite.

days.title: Rana Khalil's YouTube — Web Security Academy series + NahamSec's YouTube — Live Hacking videos
days.task: (1) Watch Rana Khalil's free playlist solving each PortSwigger lab on video, for whichever labs you personally found hardest — a different way of thinking. (2) Watch a few of NahamSec's free 'Live Hacking' videos to see the real thought process of a professional hunter working a real target.

days.title: Phase wrap-up: a portfolio of what you've solved
days.task: Compile every challenge/lab you've solved so far (Bandit, PortSwigger, Hacker101, DVWA, Natas, HackTheBox, Gruyere) into a 'Portfolio' page in Obsidian — the seed of your future resume.

phases.title: Recon & Professional Hunting Methodology
phases.subtitle: Before testing any vulnerability, map the full attack surface

days.title: Jason Haddix — Bug Hunter's Methodology (full talk) + Bug Hunter's Methodology v4 — Recon Edition
days.task: (1) Watch Jason Haddix's full 2-hour training with complete notes; one of the most respected free methodologies in bug bounty. (2) Watch the recon-focused edition of this methodology and list every tool it introduces in Obsidian.

resources.t: The Bug Hunter's Methodology — full 2-hour talk (free)
Bug Hunter's Methodology v4.0 — Recon Edition (free)

days.title: Subdomain enumeration tools
days.task: Install subfinder and amass and run them against a domain with a public bug bounty program (within program rules); compare their output.

days.title: Probing live hosts: httpx
days.task: Install httpx and pipe your subdomain list into it to see which hosts are alive, their status codes, and their tech stack.

days.title: Automated vulnerability scanning: nuclei + Content/path discovery: ffuf and wordlists
days.task: (1) Install nuclei, update its free community templates, and run it against authorized targets (within program scope); learn to spot false positives. (2) Practice ffuf for directory/content discovery with SecLists wordlists; see the practical difference between parameter, path, and subdomain fuzzing.

days.title: Tomnomnom's tools and a combined recon pipeline
days.task: Install tomnomnom's lightweight, powerful tools (waybackurls, gf, httprobe) and build a combined pipeline: subfinder | httpx | nuclei.

resources.t: waybackurls — URL discovery via web archive (free)

days.title: Google Dorking and advanced OSINT
days.task: Learn Google Dork techniques (site:, inurl:, filetype:) and OSINT for finding exposed sensitive files, admin panels, and forgotten subdomains.

days.title: Technology fingerprinting + Build your personal recon pipeline, final version
days.task: (1) Practice Wappalyzer and whatweb for identifying a target's framework, CMS, and libraries — knowing the exact tech version is a direct path to known CVEs. (2) Combine your Python tool from Phase 3 with your new tools (subfinder, httpx, nuclei) into a single Bash/Python script that runs your entire initial recon flow on one input domain.

days.title: Pick your first real bug bounty target
days.task: Based on scope, competition level, and app type, choose a real bug bounty program (HackerOne/Bugcrowd) or VDP you'll focus on in the coming phases. Read its scope and rules of engagement in full.

days.title: First full recon pass on a real target
days.task: Run your recon pipeline against your chosen target (strictly within authorized scope). Categorize the results in Obsidian: subdomains, tech stack, API endpoints, and suspicious entry points.

resources.t: Recon checklist — Voorivex Bug Bounty Roadmap

phases.title: Mobile & Advanced API Security
phases.subtitle: Many bug bounty programs today include mobile apps and APIs — less competition, often higher payouts

days.title: Intro to OWASP MASVS/MASTG + Set up an Android testing environment
days.task: (1) Review the OWASP Mobile Application Security standard (MASVS) and its testing guide (MASTG) as your mobile security roadmap. (2) Install Android Studio and an AVD (Android emulator, free), learn ADB, and install a practice vulnerable app (AndroGoat) on the emulator.

days.title: Intercepting mobile app traffic with Burp
days.task: Set Burp Suite as the emulator's proxy, install the CA certificate, and intercept AndroGoat's traffic — the exact technique for testing any real mobile app.

days.title: Decompiling and static analysis of an Android app
days.task: Decompile an APK with jadx and look for hardcoded secrets (API keys, server addresses, passwords) in the code.

days.title: Insecure data storage and SSL pinning bypass
days.task: Check what data an app stores insecurely (SharedPreferences, local DB), and learn SSL pinning and free bypass techniques (Frida/Objection).

days.title: OWASP API Security Top 10 + BOLA/IDOR in APIs
days.task: (1) Read the 2023 OWASP API Security Top 10 in full — the dedicated roadmap for API vulnerabilities, extremely valuable in bug bounty today. (2) Practice Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) — the most common real-world API bug — with PortSwigger's practical labs.

days.title: Deep-dive GraphQL security
days.task: Go deeper on introspection queries, batching attacks, and IDOR in GraphQL with PortSwigger's free labs.

days.title: APIsec University — free API security courses
days.task: Work through APIsec University's free courses, especially the introductory API Penetration Testing course.

days.title: Phase capstone: full test of a free public API
days.task: Using Postman or Burp, fully assess a public practice API (e.g. OWASP Juice Shop): enumerate every endpoint, break auth, and hunt for BOLA.

resources.t: OWASP Juice Shop — fully vulnerable practice app (free)

phases.title: Real Hunting & Professional Reporting
phases.subtitle: From here on you work real programs; report quality matters as much as the bug itself

days.title: Anatomy of a professional bug bounty report + Deep-read 10 top disclosed reports
days.task: (1) Learn the standard structure of a good report (Title, Summary, Steps to Reproduce, Impact, Remediation, PoC) from HackerOne's guide and build your own template in Obsidian. (2) Read 10 top-rated disclosed reports on HackerOne Hacktivity and analyze each: how was the bug found, why was impact high, how was the report written?

days.title: Hunt day 1: authentication and access control
days.task: On your chosen target, focus fully on authentication, session management and IDOR. Log every suspicious path in Obsidian even if you're not sure it's a bug.

days.title: Hunt day 2: input testing for XSS and injection
days.task: Fuzz every input field, URL parameter, and controllable header of the target for XSS and injection types with Burp Intruder.

days.title: Hunt day 3: business logic testing + Hunt day 4: API and mobile-related endpoints
days.task: (1) Test the target's multi-step flows (checkout, discounts, referrals, plan upgrades) for logic bugs — no scanner finds these, and they often pay well. (2) If the target has a mobile app or public API, apply your Phase 8 skills to it; otherwise go deeper on the attack surface you mapped in Phase 7's recon.

days.title: Write your first full report (even a low-severity VDP find)
days.task: Report anything you've found so far — even a low-risk bug — using the professional format you built on day one of this phase. Add a clear PoC (screenshot or short screen recording).

days.title: Learning from rejected reports (Duplicate/N-A)
days.task: Read HackerOne's docs on common rejection reasons (Duplicate, Informative, Not Applicable, Out of Scope) so you approach triage with the right mindset and don't get discouraged.

days.title: Hunt day 5: focus on one specialized vulnerability class + Expand your hunting scope: pick targets 2 and 3
days.task: (1) Pick one of the lower-competition classes you learned in Phase 5 (race conditions, SSRF, or request smuggling) and test the target specifically for it. (2) Choose two more bug bounty programs (ideally with a different tech stack than your first target) to increase your recon/testing speed and gain variety.

days.title: Sustained hunting and building a daily habit
days.task: Set a fixed daily or weekly time block for ongoing hunting. Log every finding (bug or not) in Obsidian tagged (Confirmed/Duplicate/Triaged/Rejected) to track your real progress.

days.title: Build a resume and public hunter profile
days.task: Write a short security resume and make your GitHub profile (with the recon tools you built along the way) public — this portfolio directly affects future job opportunities.

phases.title: Advanced Topics & Continuous Growth
phases.subtitle: The road doesn't 'end' here — this phase is your framework for lifelong learning

days.title: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 from a security angle + HTTP Desync Attacks and Web Cache Poisoning — the original research
days.task: (1) Read James Kettle's research on the differences between HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 and their security implications, especially for request smuggling. (2) Read James Kettle's two foundational papers on request smuggling and cache poisoning — the industry's primary references in this area.

resources.t: James Kettle — HTTP/2: The Sequel is Always Worse (free, PortSwigger Research)

days.title: Differential parsing: Orange Tsai's research
days.task: Watch/read Orange Tsai's famous 'Breaking Parser Logic' talk and the Nginx off-by-slash example — a masterclass in creative bug-finding.

resources.t: Orange Tsai — Breaking Parser Logic slides (free, GitHub)

days.title: Reverse proxies and weird proxy behavior + OAuth 2.0 in depth
days.task: (1) Review Aleksei Tiurin's 'weird_proxies' research on unexpected reverse-proxy behavior — inspiration for finding custom bugs in complex architectures. (2) Review deeper OAuth concepts (Authorization Code Flow, PKCE, state parameter) so you can spot more complex OAuth bugs too.

days.title: Build your own vulnerable app with a framework
days.task: Build a small app with Django or Laravel (both free) and deliberately plant a few vulnerabilities — building a bug yourself deepens your understanding of exploiting it.

days.title: Web LLM Attacks — going deeper
days.task: Revisit PortSwigger's Web LLM Attacks labs and follow new research on prompt injection — this field is evolving fast.

days.title: Enter a real CTF + Follow daily web security news
days.task: (1) Sign up for a free, public CTF competition (via CTFtime) and spend at least a few hours working web challenges, solo or with a team. (2) Build a daily news-source list (top researchers on X, free newsletters like tl;dr sec) and turn it into a 15-minute daily habit.

days.title: Final review and update of your personal methodology
days.task: Revisit and rewrite the Methodology document you started on day one in Obsidian. It should now be a fully personalized hunting methodology you follow on every engagement.

resources.t: Voorivex Bug Bounty Roadmap — for final inspiration

days.title: Final wrap-up and your next 6 months
days.task: Write a final document: what you learned, which vulnerability classes you're strongest in, and your plan for the next 6 months (specializing in one area, joining private programs, or an AppSec career path). This isn't the end — it's the starting point of your professional hunting career.

resources.t: NahamSec's full resource list to keep going

phases.title: AI in Bug Bounty
phases.subtitle: AI is both a new attack surface you must understand, and a tool that will wreck your reputation if you misuse it

days.title: The real state of AI in bug bounty today
days.task: Start with facts, not hype: most professional hunters today use AI to speed up recon, code analysis, and report writing — but low-quality 'AI slop' reports have made programs like curl shut down their bug bounty entirely. Fully understand this tension before you use AI yourself.

resources.t: HackerOne — official blog on AI and Hai
Google Project Zero — a real vulnerability found by AI (Big Sleep)

days.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
days.task: Read OWASP's official, free list of LLM application vulnerabilities (Prompt Injection, Insecure Output Handling, Training Data Poisoning, etc.) in full — the reference framework for this entire phase.

resources.t: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (free, official)

days.title: Hands-on prompt injection: the Gandalf game
days.task: Solve Lakera's free, interactive Gandalf game from level zero to the final level (Gandalf the White). The best free way in the world to build a hands-on intuition for prompt injection, not just theory.

days.title: Revisit PortSwigger Web LLM Attacks with an attacker mindset
days.task: Return to the Web LLM Attacks labs you solved in the core vulnerabilities phase, but this time focus on indirect prompt injection (when the payload is injected from a third-party source like an email or web page) and chaining it with SSRF/exfiltration.

resources.t: Embrace The Red — independent prompt injection research (free)

days.title: Specialized free resource: Simon Willison's blog
days.task: Simon Willison is one of the most respected independent voices in LLM security. Read his full free prompt-injection tag archive — he was the first to precisely formalize this attack class.

days.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol) security — the 2026 emerging attack surface
days.task: MCP is the standard protocol connecting tools to AI models and is fast becoming a serious attack surface (command injection, tool poisoning, over-permissioned access). Read the official security docs and understand why dozens of CVEs have hit MCP servers in the past few months.

days.title: AI as a recon assistant: summarizing and prioritizing targets
days.task: Feed the raw output of one of your earlier scans (subfinder/httpx/nuclei) to a language model (Claude or similar, free tier) and ask it to summarize, categorize, and risk-prioritize the output. This saves hours of manual log analysis — but always verify the model's output with your own eyes.

resources.t: Anthropic — official Claude docs (free to start)

days.title: AI as a code review assistant
days.task: Review a small open-source project (or your own vulnerable app from Phase 10) with AI help, looking for unsafe patterns (SQL string concatenation, eval on user input, uncontrolled file paths); then re-check the findings with the free open-source tool Semgrep to see what the model got right or wrong.

resources.t: Semgrep — free open-source static analysis tool

days.title: Writing reports with AI — correctly, not as slop
days.task: Learn to use AI to polish the writing, structure, and clarity of reports for bugs you found entirely by hand and manually verified — never to fabricate a finding. Read HackerOne's Good Faith AI Research rules in full to understand where the legal/ethical line is.

resources.t: HackerOne — Good Faith AI Research Safe Harbor

days.title: Phase capstone: an AI helper script for your methodology
days.task: Write a small Python script that takes the output of your Phase 7 recon.py, uses a free/cheap language model API to do a first-pass categorization, and saves a Markdown summary report. Add this tool to your personal GitHub repo.

resources.t: Anthropic API — docs (free to start, pay-as-you-go)
